title: After her indictment, could this Baltimore senator be unseated?
summary: After her federal indictment on blackmailing charges in late 2025, Maryland Sen. Dalya Attar (D-Baltimore City) faces a formidable opponent in Del. Malcolm Ruff (D-Baltimore City) who now has the governor’s backing and a fundraising edge.
content:
by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters June 15, 2026

by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters June 15, 2026

After her federal indictment on blackmailing charges in late 2025, Maryland Sen. Dalya Attar (D-Baltimore City) faces a formidable opponent in Del. Malcolm Ruff (D-Baltimore City) who now has the governor’s backing and a fundraising edge.

The senator’s backers say Attar, a criminal defense attorney who is also the first Orthodox Jewish woman to serve in the Senate, has shown she can effectively represent the various communities in the sprawling Northwest Baltimore district, even amid scandal.

The delegate’s supporters say Ruff, a Black civil rights and defense attorney, is a stronger candidate to represent the majority-Black district in Maryland’s largest city, with or without Attar’s indictment.

The outcome of the June 23 Democratic primary could be considered a litmus test for the effect of Attar’s criminal case on her political future. After the indictment, Senate leaders did not formally discipline Attar, or call for her resignation, and she served throughout the most recent 90-day session in Annapolis.

“My interest is whose platform represents — and whose political and policy track record represents — what’s in the best interest of Black people,” said Dayvon Love, the public policy director for Leaders of a Beautiful Struggle, a Baltimore-based think tank that chose Ruff for its first-ever political endorsement. “Delegate Ruff’s platform is pretty clearly more on that progressive flank that’s going to be more beneficial to Black people.”

During the race, tensions have at times boiled over between the district’s Black and its Orthodox Jewish communities, both vying for one of their own to hold the district’s most powerful seat. Accusations of antisemitism have been lodged against a prominent Ruff supporter, who took issue with a plea from rabbinical leaders for local Orthodox Jews to change their party if needed to vote in the closed primary.

“It’s unfortunate,” said Howard Libit, executive director of the Baltimore Jewish Council. “The race is taking an ugly turn.”

Neither Attar nor Ruff agreed to an interview for this story.

The district, which is 63% Black, sweeps from north Baltimore’s wealthy and majority-white Roland Park over to the majority-Black neighborhoods encircling Pimlico Race Course, and also includes the majority-Black westernmost swath of the city, all the way down to St, Agnes Hospital. It also includes much of the region’s Orthodox Jewish community, said Evan Serpick, a Ruff supporter who is also running for Democratic Central Committee.

“It’s just a very large district. It stretches from very disparate parts of the city,” said Serpick, a Jewish man who has resided in the district, in Mount Washington, for nearly two decades.

Attar has the backing of longtime Del. Sandy Rosenberg, who has represented the 41st District since January 1983, and Del. Sean Stinnett, who was appointed to the seat in 2025. The three lawmakers are running as a ticket.

“I’m doing door-to-door on behalf of the ticket — all three of us are — and I think people are aware of how we, both as individual members and as a team, have been advocates for the entire district,” Rosenberg said.

It’s an advantage, Rosenberg said, that voters have elected both him and Attar in the past. But they have never seen Ruff on the ballot: He was appointed in 2023 to fill a vacancy left behind when Del. Tony Bridges (D-Baltimore City) took a role in Gov. Wes Moore’s (D) administration. The Democratic Central Committee deadlocked 4-4 between Ruff and another candidate, and it was Moore who broke the tie, selecting Ruff.

Rosenberg said he’s feeling “very positive” about voters’ reaction to the ticket, and that he’s not hearing much about Attar’s indictment while knocking on doors around the district.

Attar, her brother and a former Baltimore City police officer were all charged in October with carrying out a blackmail scheme to videotape a consultant, with whom Attar had a political disagreement, having an affair, then use the recordings to threaten the consultant.

The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.

“This reinforces what I learned 44 years ago when I first ran, when my advisers would say, ‘We’ve got to worry about this, we’ve got to worry about that,’” Rosenberg said. “And I would say, ‘Let me leave this room.’”

But campaign finance records tell a troubling story for Attar.

As of mid-May, the last time the candidates filed campaign finance reports, Ruff had received about $493,000 in total contributions, and had about $104,000 left on hand. Attar, by comparison, had received $213,000 and had $76,000 left in the bank.

Ruff received a boost in early May when he received the endorsement of Moore, who is also providing financial support, having added Ruff to his “Leave No One Behind” slate later that same month.

“Malcolm Ruff is a fighter, a proven leader and exactly the kind of champion Baltimore needs in Annapolis,” said Moore in a statement shared by his campaign.

It’s not the first time Ruff and Attar have faced off. In January 2025, when both were delegates, they vied for the Senate seat vacated by Sen. Jill Carter (D-Baltimore City), whom Moore appointed to the Board of Contract Appeals. That time, Attar won out, in a 5-3 vote of the Baltimore City Democratic Central Committee.

Stinnett said he urged Ruff against running for Senate, arguing that Ruff hadn’t run a typical campaign yet. Stinnett said he opted to stick with the incumbents in Attar and Rosenberg, feeling that it would give him an advantage in the race.

”This is going to be the best way for me to get elected instead of me being on a no-name, no-experience ticket,” Stinnett said.

As for Attar’s indictment, Stinnett said she ought to be considered innocent until she is proven guilty.

“Until the judge says otherwise, I’m going to continue doing what I’m doing, and stick with my team.”

Stinnett, who is Black, said he’s been the subject of “unfortunate” name-calling attacks from some members of the Black community because of his choice to run with Attar.

“I’m being called a sell-out, Uncle Tom, a traitor — just because I chose to run with the incumbents, and that gives me the best opportunity to win,” Stinnett said.

The atmosphere in the district is charged. Carter, who has commented frequently about the race online, has been accused of antisemitism, by the editorial board of The Baltimore Sun, and by online Jewish publication Jmore, in a piece by activist and attorney Jay Bernstein.

They took issue with Carter’s remarks online that leaders in the Orthodox community were endeavoring to “control the politics” of the majority Black district.

But Carter has argued her online comments were not antisemitic at all, but a legitimate criticism of political activities.

“The commentary at issue did not concern Jews as a people. It did not concern Judaism as a faith. It did not concern Jewish history, culture or identity,” Carter wrote in a response letter shared with Maryland Matters. “It concerned political conduct and political influence in a majority-Black legislative district.”

“This is an important race. I feel that we are fighting very much for our political lives in this 41st District race,” Carter said in an interview.

She pointed to a 2022 slate for Democratic Central Committee that included only members of the Orthodox community, and a recent push by rabbinical leaders to encourage members of the Orthodox community to change their political party if necessary to vote in closed primary races.

YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE.

“The Primary Election next month is an absolutely critical moment for our community,” reads the notice from the Baltimore Rabbinical Council, or Vaad Harabbonim, publishes in the Baltimore Scoop online publication. “Do not let your vote go to waste.”

“It’s saying: Abandon your principles,” Carter said.

To Love, of Leaders of a Beautiful Struggle, Ruff’s standing on juvenile justice issues sets him apart as a voice for the Black community. Ruff was among eight Democrats who voted against a bill in 2024 that made a number of changes to juvenile justice, including that children ages 10 to 12 could be sent to juvenile court if charged for certain offenses.

“That’s one example of a clear difference in terms of policy perspective that I think is demonstrative of them reflecting two different wings to the Democratic Party,” Love said.

But Stinnett points to Attar’s ability to deliver resources to various parts of the district, including by supporting improvement projects at the Ambassador Theater and Penhurst Park.

“I think that she’s provided a lot of resources and a lot of things to the community, whether it be Black, white, Jewish, Muslim,” Stinnett said.

Serpick says he takes issue with a vote from Attar about abortion. In 2022, she voted against the Abortion Care Access Act, which expanded the number of providers in Maryland authorized to provide an abortion. When Gov. Larry Hogan (R), vetoed the measure, Attar voted against overriding his veto, though the bill ultimately became law.

Her indictment is also influencing his choice to vote for Ruff, especially given that another state senator representing the district, Sen. Nathaniel T. Oaks (D-Baltimore City) was indicted and found guilty on wire fraud charges in 2018, which Serpick called an “embarrassment.”

“I’m really eager to have someone who I think we can all really be proud of,” Serpick said, “And who I really hope can bring the district together.”
